content: The metre per second (m/s) is a derived unit in the International System of Units (SI) used to measure both speed (a scalar quantity) and velocity (a vector quantity that includes both magnitude and direction). It is defined as the distance traveled in metres divided by the time taken in seconds. The official SI abbreviation for this unit is m·s⁻¹ or equivalently m/s, although the informal abbreviation mps is sometimes used in casual contexts. In cases where the metre per second is not a practical unit due to the scale of measurement, such as in astronomical observations, velocities are often expressed in kilometres per second (km/s). One kilometre per second is equivalent to 1,000 metres per second. In non-scientific literature, the abbreviation kps is occasionally used instead of km/s. To provide a relatable example, one metre per second is approximately the speed at which an average person walks. On the other hand, 1 kilometre per second (or 1,000 metres per second) is a much faster velocity, often used in contexts like space travel or astrophysics. It is worth noting that while m·s⁻¹ is a derived SI unit, it can be considered more fundamental than the metre itself. This is because the definition of the metre is based on the speed of light in a vacuum, which is precisely defined as 299,792,458 m·s⁻¹. Consequently, one metre is defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.
